title: AML/CFT Compliance Professional
tagline: Follow the money, spot the risk and report it right: practical AML, CFT and sanctions compliance for Pakistan's financial sector.
description:
Every account you open, every remittance you pay and every trade document you check is a point where criminals and terrorist financiers try to get in. This certification builds the judgement that front-line and compliance staff need to keep them out, and to stay on the right side of Pakistan's law and its regulators.

You will learn how money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing actually work, how the **FATF standards** and **Pakistan's framework** (the Anti-Money Laundering Act 2010, the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997, the Financial Monitoring Unit, SBP and SECP regulations) fit together, and why Pakistan's grey-list years still shape supervision today.

The course is built around practice, not theory: risk-rating real-looking customers, unwrapping ownership structures, reviewing PEP and NPO relationships, investigating alerts, spotting trade-based laundering, writing a strong suspicious transaction report without tipping off the customer, and handling a sanctions match from first alert to freeze.

Five stages, ten-question tests after each, and a tough timed final exam built from realistic Pakistani scenarios.
audience: Branch, operations and customer-service staff in banks and microfinance banks who open accounts and handle cash
Compliance, AML and sanctions analysts who review alerts, PEPs and high-risk customers
Trade finance, remittance and treasury staff who process cross-border payments
Staff of exchange companies, insurers, brokers, fintechs and payment service providers
Real estate agents, jewellers, accountants and other DNFBPs with AML/CFT obligations
Internal auditors and risk managers who test AML/CFT controls
outcomes: Explain how money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing work and how FATF and Pakistan's laws respond to them
Apply the risk-based approach to rate customers, products, geographies and channels and to justify the result
Perform customer due diligence, identify beneficial owners and decide when simplified or enhanced measures apply
Recognise red flags in branches, trade, remittances and digital channels and investigate alerts in a disciplined way
Escalate and report suspicions correctly, write a clear STR narrative and avoid tipping off
Screen against UN and domestic lists and act on a true match by freezing and reporting without delay
Describe the parts of an effective compliance programme and the consequences when it fails

quest.name: Follow the Rupee
quest.premise: You have just joined the financial crime desk of a mid-sized Pakistani bank. On your first morning, Chief Compliance Officer Ayesha Siddiqui hands you a file: cash deposits in Multan, wallet transfers in Karachi, an export invoice from Faisalabad and a remittance from the Gulf that all seem to connect. With analyst Hamza Baloch, branch manager Rukhsana Memon and trade officer Neha Gill, master five stages to follow the rupee, then face the final boss: presenting your case to the board.

badge.name: Rupee Tracker
badge.description: Awarded to compliance professionals who can follow the money, judge the risk, report it right and freeze it fast.

cast.name: Kamran Sheikh
cast.role: Head of Retail and Priority Banking

sessions.title: Dirty Money, Terror Funds and the Rules of the Game
sessions.summary: Before you can follow the money, you need the map: how laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing work, why they matter to Pakistan, and which international standards, laws and authorities shape your obligations.
objectives: Describe the three stages of money laundering and recognise them in Pakistani scenarios
Distinguish terrorist financing and proliferation financing from money laundering
Explain the role of FATF, its Recommendations and mutual evaluations, and Pakistan's grey-list history
Map Pakistan's AML/CFT laws and the roles of the FMU, SBP, SECP and other supervisors

cards.title: Day one: the file on your desk
cards.setting: Financial crime desk, head office, I.I. Chundrigar Road, Karachi. 9:05 am.

lines.text: Your new badge still smells of the laminator when a thick brown file lands on your desk.
Welcome to the desk. I am Ayesha Siddiqui, and I don't believe in easing people in. This file is your first case.
Cash deposits in Multan. A cluster of wallets in Karachi. An export invoice from Faisalabad. A 'family gift' from the Gulf. I think they are one trail.
Hamza, senior analyst. The Multan account belongs to a small mobile shop owner, Irfan Bhatti. Strangers deposit cash for him in three cities.
(on speakerphone from Multan) Rukhsana here, branch manager. My tellers say the depositors don't even know what Irfan sells. Something is off.
And within a day the money is gone: wallets in Karachi, then a new firm called Zarnab Trading. Classic movement, or just a busy shopkeeper?
That is exactly the question. Before you follow the rupee, you need the map: how dirty money moves, who sets the rules, and who does what in Pakistan.
Stage one is the Map Room. Ready to read the trail like an investigator?

scenes.heading: It starts with a crime
scenes.narration: Every laundering case begins with a crime that produces money: corruption, smuggling, drugs, fraud, tax evasion. We call that underlying crime the predicate offence.

scenes.heading: Stage one: placement
scenes.narration: First, the criminal has to get the money into the system. Cash is deposited in small amounts, mixed with a shop's genuine takings, or turned into gold and prize bonds. That is placement.

scenes.heading: Stage two: layering
scenes.narration: Next, the money is moved again and again: to relatives, to front companies, abroad and back. Each hop makes the trail harder to follow. That is layering.

scenes.heading: Stage three: integration
scenes.narration: Finally, the money comes home looking respectable: a plot, a car, a 'consultancy fee' or a 'loan' from a friendly company. That is integration.

scenes.heading: A model, not a rulebook
scenes.narration: Real cases skip stages or run them at once. Fraud money is often already in a bank, so it starts at layering. Your job is not perfect labels. It is spotting activity with no sensible purpose.

scenes.heading: Two crimes, one person
scenes.narration: Laundering is a separate offence from the predicate crime. A smuggler who launders his own profits can be charged for both. That is called self-laundering.

cards.title: The three stages, Pakistani style
cards.caption: Most laundering cases can be mapped on these three steps, even when the stages overlap.

items.label: Predicate crime
items.detail: Bribes, smuggling, drug sales, fraud or tax evasion generate proceeds.

items.label: Placement
items.detail: Cash enters the system: split deposits, third-party depositors, mixing with genuine shop takings.

items.label: Layering
items.detail: Rapid transfers among relatives, front firms, wallets and foreign accounts to break the audit trail.

items.label: Integration
items.detail: Funds return as plots, cars, business investment or 'loans' and 'fees' that look legitimate.

cards.title: Match the move to the term
cards.prompt: Link each term to the example from Ayesha's training archive that best illustrates it.

pairs.right: A cloth trader mixes cash from smuggled goods into his daily shop takings and deposits the total each evening.
Bribe money is bounced between three relatives' accounts and a cousin's 'construction' firm.
The same firm later pays the official a 'consultancy fee', which he uses to buy a house.
The customs fraud that produced the money in the first place.
A drug trafficker personally moves his own proceeds through his rice company as 'profit'.

cards.question: A property dealer in Lahore receives cash from a land-grabbing gang, deposits it as 'token money' from buyers, then wires it to two cousins, who later 'lend' it back to buy a commercial plot. Which part of this chain is integration?
options: Depositing the cash as token money
Wiring the funds to the cousins
The 'loan' from the cousins used to buy the plot
The land grabbing itself
cards.explanation: Integration is when the money comes back looking legitimate, here as a family 'loan' that funds an asset. The deposit is placement, the wires to cousins are layering, and the land grabbing is the predicate offence.

cards.title: Small money, big danger
cards.setting: Analysts' corner, 11:30 am. Hamza turns his screen towards you.

lines.text: Look at this side branch of the trail. One Karachi wallet sends PKR 20,000 every month to a 'welfare' collector. Tiny amounts.
The sender is a salaried engineer. Clean salary, clean employer. So no laundering, right?
Wrong question. Terrorist financing is about where money goes, not where it came from. Clean salary can still fund a banned group under a new name.
No attack has to happen first, and any individual can commit it. Big-value thresholds will never catch PKR 20,000 a month. Behaviour and connections will.
(joining the call from Faisalabad) And I have a third kind for you. A trading firm asked about an LC for vacuum pumps, routed through a free-trade hub, end user keeps changing.
That smells like proliferation financing: dual-use goods, a vague end user, indirect routing. Three risks, three different questions. Let's learn to tell them apart.

cards.title: ML, TF and PF: three different questions
cards.body:
| | Money laundering | Terrorist financing | Proliferation financing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Key question | Where did it **come from**? | Where is it **going**? | What will it **buy**, for whom? |
| Source | Criminal | Legal **or** criminal | Usually commercial |
| Size | Often large | Often **small** | Varies, trade-linked |

- **TF** is providing or collecting funds for terrorist acts, organisations or individual terrorists, even with no specific attack linked. Watch charities used as fronts, banned groups under new names, cash couriers, hawala and small wallet transfers.
- **PF** funds weapons of mass destruction programmes. It hides in trade: **dual-use goods**, front companies, false end users, transshipment hubs and third-party payers.

That is why Pakistan's regulations speak of **AML/CFT/CPF**.

cards.title: ML, TF or PF?
cards.prompt: Sort each case from the bank's alert archive into the risk it raises most directly.

items.text: A tax officer's salary account receives large cash deposits far beyond his pay
Small monthly wallet transfers from salaried donors to a collector for a banned group's new front
A new firm buys machine tools for an undisclosed end user via a transshipment hub
Smuggling profits are deposited by several strangers into a shop owner's account
A cash courier carries donations collected in mosques to a proscribed outfit
Vacuum pumps ordered for a changing end user, paid by an unrelated third party
Fraud proceeds bounced through relatives' accounts, then used to buy plots
A 'relief' NPO sends funds to an area unrelated to its projects, office bearers linked to a banned group

cards.title: Pakistan's FATF journey
cards.caption: Exit from the grey list came from evidence that controls work. The next mutual evaluation will test that again.

items.label: FATF founded by the G7
items.detail: Sets global AML standards; later adds TF and PF. Pakistan is assessed through the Asia/Pacific Group (APG).

items.label: Recommendations revised
items.detail: The 40 Recommendations are comprehensively revised. Pakistan is also under increased monitoring from 2012 to 2015.

items.label: Grey-listed again
items.detail: Mainly over TF risk. Pakistan commits to a 27-item action plan focused on terrorist financing.

items.label: APG mutual evaluation
items.detail: Finds wider weaknesses in technical compliance and effectiveness.

items.label: Reform years
items.detail: Law amendments, stronger SBP/SECP supervision, DNFBPs brought under supervision, action on hawala, more TF cases.

items.label: Second action plan
items.detail: A further 7-item plan focused mainly on money laundering.

items.label: Removed from grey list
items.detail: Both plans judged substantially complete after an on-site visit.

items.label: Future mutual evaluations
items.detail: Effectiveness will be tested again, file by file, branch by branch.

cards.front: Technical compliance
cards.back: Are the laws, regulations and enforceable measures in place to meet each FATF Recommendation? The 'on paper' rating.

cards.front: Effectiveness
cards.back: Is the system actually producing results, such as investigations, confiscations, freezes and quality STRs? Rated against 11 Immediate Outcomes.

cards.front: Which countries get both ratings?
cards.back: Every assessed country, listed or not. Good laws with few results still mean a low effectiveness rating.

cards.front: Grey list (increased monitoring)
cards.back: The country works through an agreed action plan. No legal ban follows, but foreign banks add scrutiny, so costs and correspondent pressure rise.

cards.front: Black list (call for action)
cards.back: FATF calls on members to apply enhanced due diligence and, in the most serious cases, countermeasures. FATF listing itself is not UN sanctions.

cards.front: Why do assessors visit branches?
cards.back: Effectiveness depends on whether front-line staff actually apply CDD and escalate concerns day to day, not just on head-office policy.

cards.question: Assessors find that a country's AML laws closely follow the FATF Recommendations, but its FIU's reports rarely lead to prosecutions and almost nothing is confiscated. What is the most likely finding?
options: Low technical compliance, because more laws are needed
A weak effectiveness rating, because the laws are not producing results
Automatic black-listing with countermeasures
No issue, because effectiveness is only assessed for listed countries
cards.explanation: Effectiveness is assessed separately from technical compliance: sound laws that produce few cases and little confiscation signal an effectiveness gap. Writing more laws would not fix an implementation problem, and every assessed country is rated on both dimensions.

cards.title: 'We're off the grey list now'
cards.setting: Lift lobby, 1:15 pm. Kamran Sheikh, head of retail, steps in beside you.

lines.text: So you're Ayesha's new recruit. Friendly advice: we left the grey list in 2022. SBP will care about capital and NPLs now, not AML forms.
Kamran, that is a myth I hear every week. Every country faces periodic mutual evaluations, listed or not, and effectiveness will be tested again.
SBP and SECP keep inspecting and keep penalising. And money laundering controls matter as much as TF controls; the 2021 plan was mostly about ML.
Fine, fine. But who actually checks us? The FMU?
No. The FMU is the intelligence unit that receives our reports. SBP supervises us. Our new colleague is about to learn exactly who does what.

cards.title: Pakistan's AML/CFT laws at a glance
cards.caption: You do not need section numbers. You do need to know what each law is for.

items.label: AMLA
items.left: Anti-Money Laundering Act 2010 (as amended, notably in 2020)
items.right: Criminalises ML, creates the FMU, sets CDD, records, STR/CTR duties and the tipping-off ban

items.label: ATA
items.right: Criminalises TF; proscription of organisations (First Schedule) and persons (Fourth Schedule); freezing of their funds

items.label: UNSC Act
items.right: Gives effect to UN Security Council sanctions, including asset freezes, through government orders

items.label: FX law
items.right: Relevant to unlicensed money transfer such as hawala and hundi

items.label: Export control
items.right: Controls sensitive and dual-use goods; key for proliferation financing

items.label: Regulations
items.right: Turn the laws into detailed, enforceable rules for the institutions each supervises

cards.title: Who does what?
cards.prompt: Match each body to its main AML/CFT role in Pakistan.

pairs.right: Pakistan's FIU: receives and analyses STRs and CTRs from all reporting entities and passes intelligence to investigators
Supervises banks, microfinance banks, exchange companies and the payment and e-money firms it licenses
Supervises securities brokers, insurers, NBFCs and modarabas; holds company and beneficial ownership information
Supervises real estate agents and dealers in precious metals and stones

pairs.left: Law enforcement (FIA, CTDs, NAB, ANF, Customs)
pairs.right: Investigate and prosecute ML, TF and predicate crimes
Publishes the lists of proscribed organisations and persons under the ATA

cards.title: The 'urgent' WhatsApp request
cards.situation: Rukhsana forwards you a message. A caller claiming to be from a law enforcement agency phoned her Multan teller, asking for Irfan Bhatti's last six months of statements 'urgently, on WhatsApp, before 5 pm'. He sounded official and mentioned the case number. The teller has the statement ready to send. What do you advise?

choices.text: Send it. Agencies have legal powers, and delaying could obstruct an investigation.
choices.outcome: The statement goes to an unverified number. A week later it turns out the caller was a fixer working for Irfan's associates, who now know the bank is looking. You have leaked data and possibly tipped off the subject.

choices.text: Route the request to compliance, which verifies the requester's identity and legal authority and responds through proper channels.
choices.outcome: Compliance contacts the agency through official channels. The request turns out to be genuine, and a formal written request arrives within days. Records are shared lawfully, with a clean audit trail. This is the right route.

choices.text: Refuse permanently. Customer records can never be shared with any authority.
choices.outcome: Authorities do have lawful powers to obtain records. A flat refusal creates friction and could obstruct a legitimate case. The right answer is verification, not refusal.

choices.text: Tell the caller to ask the FMU, since only the FMU can request records.
choices.outcome: Partly cautious, but wrong on the law: other agencies also have lawful access powers. You still need compliance to verify and handle the request properly.

cards.title: Why it matters: country, bank and you
cards.body:
**For Pakistan:** grey-listing brought extra checks from foreign banks, pressure on correspondent relationships, higher trade and remittance costs and cautious investors.

**For the bank:** penalties, business restrictions, remediation orders, lost correspondent banks and years of reputational damage.

**For you personally:**
- Knowingly helping launder money is an offence.
- **Tipping off** a customer about a report is an offence.
- Overriding controls for a valued client can bring disciplinary, regulatory or criminal consequences.

**The protective side:** good-faith reporting is protected by law, and a clear file note that says what you saw and why you escalated is your best shield.

cards.question: A securities broker regulated by SECP spots a client paying for large share purchases with cash deposited by unrelated third parties. Where does the broker report its suspicion, and who checks its AML/CFT compliance?
options: It reports to SECP, and the FMU supervises it
It reports to the FMU, and SECP supervises it
It reports to SBP, and SBP supervises it
It reports to the FIA, and NACTA supervises it
cards.explanation: Every reporting entity files STRs with the FMU, Pakistan's financial intelligence unit. SECP is the AML/CFT supervisor for brokers, insurers and NBFCs. The FMU is not a supervisor, and NACTA publishes proscription lists rather than supervising firms.

cards.title: Build your own source library
cards.body: Rules change through new regulations, circulars, FAQs and list updates. Bookmark the official sites of **SBP**, the **FMU**, **SECP**, **NACTA** and the **Ministry of Foreign Affairs**, and find out how your compliance team circulates updates. When this course says 'check the current instructions', that is a real step in your job, not a disclaimer.

cards.title: Map Room cleared
items: Laundering runs placement, layering, integration, but real cases skip and overlap stages; it is a separate crime, so self-laundering is chargeable.
TF is about where money goes: it can be small and come from clean sources. PF hides in trade through dual-use goods and vague end users.
FATF rates technical compliance and effectiveness for every country; Pakistan was grey-listed June 2018 to October 2022 and will be tested again.
AMLA 2010 covers ML and reporting duties, ATA 1997 covers TF and proscription, the UN (Security Council) Act 1948 gives effect to UN sanctions.
The FMU receives and analyses reports; SBP and SECP supervise; FBR covers real estate and jewellers; law enforcement investigates.
Any request for records goes through compliance to verify legal authority.

cards.prompt: Think about the products your own team handles. At which point could a criminal or terrorist financier most easily get money into, through or out of your institution, and who on your team would be the first to notice?

quiz.question: A wholesale cloth trader in Karachi mixes cash from smuggled goods with his genuine daily shop takings and deposits the total each evening. Which stage of money laundering does this most clearly represent?
options: Integration, because once mixed into a legitimate business the money already looks like ordinary trading income
Placement, because criminal cash is entering the financial system disguised as business receipts
Layering, because mixing criminal cash with genuine takings is itself the step that breaks the audit trail
None, because the trader runs a real business
quiz.explanation: Depositing criminal cash mixed with genuine takings is placement: the proceeds enter the banking system looking like sales. Layering involves moving funds through further transactions to break the trail. A genuine business can still be used to launder.

quiz.question: Which feature most clearly distinguishes terrorist financing from money laundering?
options: Terrorist financing always involves cross-border wire transfers
Terrorist financing is only committed by proscribed organisations, not individuals
Terrorist financing requires the funds to have been used in a completed attack before any offence or report arises
Terrorist financing can use funds from legitimate sources, because the concern is their destination
quiz.explanation: TF is defined by the purpose of the funds, so donations, salaries and business profits can all be TF. It does not require a completed attack, can be committed by any individual, and frequently uses domestic channels.

quiz.question: In a FATF mutual evaluation, what does an 'effectiveness' rating measure?
options: How well the country's AML/CFT system achieves results in practice, assessed against Immediate Outcomes
Whether the country has enacted the laws, regulations and enforceable measures needed to cover each FATF Recommendation
The number of banks that have adopted automated monitoring systems
Whether the country has paid its contributions to its FATF-style regional body and attended plenary meetings regularly
quiz.explanation: Effectiveness measures whether the system delivers results in practice, for example investigations, convictions, freezes and quality supervision, against 11 Immediate Outcomes. Whether laws exist on paper is technical compliance, a separate rating.

quiz.question: Which statement about Pakistan's most recent period on FATF's list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring is accurate?
options: Pakistan was listed in 2015 and removed in 2018 after completing a single action plan focused on terrorist financing
Pakistan was placed on the call-for-action list in 2018 and faced countermeasures from FATF members until 2022
Pakistan was listed in June 2018 and removed in October 2022 after completing two action plans
Pakistan was listed in 2020 because of proliferation financing concerns only
quiz.explanation: Pakistan was grey-listed in June 2018 and removed in October 2022 after completing the 2018 TF-focused action plan and the 2021 ML-focused action plan. It was under increased monitoring (grey list), not on the call-for-action (black) list.

quiz.question: A trading company imports 'industrial vacuum pumps' through a free-trade hub for an end user whose identity keeps changing, and payment comes from an unrelated third party. Which risk does this pattern raise most directly?
options: Tax evasion through customs undervaluation only
Proliferation financing, because the goods may be dual-use and the end user is unclear
Terrorist financing, because third-party payments routed through a free-trade hub are the most common TF method
Market manipulation in the securities market
quiz.explanation: Dual-use goods, indirect routing, an unclear end user and third-party payment are classic proliferation financing indicators. Nothing suggests small amounts or terrorism links, and undervaluation alone would not explain the changing end user.

quiz.question: Which law is Pakistan's main legal basis for criminalising terrorist financing and for proscribing organisations and persons?
options: The Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997
The Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010
The United Nations (Security Council) Act, 1948
The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947
quiz.explanation: The ATA 1997 criminalises TF and provides for proscription of organisations and persons with related freezing. AMLA covers money laundering and reporting duties; the UN (Security Council) Act gives effect to UN sanctions; foreign exchange law addresses matters such as unlicensed money transfer.

quiz.question: Sunil, a branch officer, receives a call from someone claiming to be from a law enforcement agency asking for a customer's statement 'urgently, by WhatsApp'. What should he do?
options: Send the statement promptly, because law enforcement agencies have legal powers to obtain records and delay could obstruct them
Refuse permanently, because customer records can never be shared with any authority
Ask the caller to email the FMU, since only the FMU can request records
Route the request to the compliance function so it can verify the legal authority before anything is shared
quiz.explanation: Authorities can lawfully obtain records, but staff must not share data on an unverified informal request. Compliance checks the requester's identity and legal authority and responds through proper channels. Refusing every request is wrong, and the FMU is not the only body with access powers.

quiz.question: Which body supervises a licensed exchange company in Pakistan for AML/CFT compliance?
options: The Financial Monitoring Unit
The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan
The State Bank of Pakistan
The Federal Board of Revenue
quiz.explanation: Exchange companies are licensed and supervised by SBP. The FMU receives their reports but is not their supervisor; SECP supervises securities, insurance and NBFC sectors; FBR's DNFBP role relates to sectors such as real estate and precious metals dealers.

quiz.question: A senior colleague says: 'Since Pakistan left the grey list in 2022, supervisors will focus on prudential issues and AML inspections will ease.' What is the best response?
options: Agree, because FATF only reviews countries that are on a public list
Disagree: future mutual evaluations will test effectiveness again, and supervisors continue AML/CFT inspections and penalties
Agree partly: after exit only terrorist financing controls remain a supervisory focus, since the action plans were TF-driven
Disagree, because Pakistan is still on the grey list under a new action plan
quiz.explanation: All countries undergo periodic mutual evaluations whether or not they are listed, and effectiveness will be tested again. Supervision and enforcement continue. Pakistan was removed in October 2022, so the claim that it remains listed is wrong, and ML controls matter as much as TF controls.

quiz.question: Why does FATF's assessment of a country look at both technical compliance and effectiveness?
options: Because effectiveness only applies to countries already on the grey list
Because technical compliance covers financial institutions while effectiveness covers only law enforcement
Because a country can have sound laws that are not applied in practice, so real-world results must also be tested
Because technical compliance is assessed by the FIU and effectiveness by the central bank
quiz.explanation: Laws on paper do not guarantee outcomes. FATF separately checks whether the framework produces results, such as quality STRs, investigations, confiscation and supervision. Both ratings apply to every assessed country and are made by the assessment team, not by domestic agencies.

sessions.title: The Risk-Based Approach: Seeing Where the Danger Lies
sessions.summary: From the watchtower you see the whole landscape. Learn how institutions assess their ML/TF/PF risk, how customer, product, geography and channel factors combine into a risk rating, and how ratings drive the controls you apply.
objectives: Explain the risk-based approach, inherent risk, controls and residual risk
Describe the steps of an enterprise-wide risk assessment and how it links to Pakistan's national risk assessment
Assess customer, product/service, geographic and delivery channel risk factors
Assign and justify customer risk ratings and explain what each rating triggers
Distinguish sound risk management from wholesale de-risking

cards.title: A map that is four years old
cards.setting: The 14th-floor meeting room everyone calls the Watchtower. Monday, 10 am.

lines.text: Stage two. Before we chase Irfan's cash any further, ask a bigger question: why didn't our own systems shout louder about it?
I pulled the enterprise risk assessment. Last updated four years ago, before we launched wallets and SME trade finance.
It rates our app-onboarding channel as low risk. Yet 80 percent of last year's STRs came from accounts opened through that channel.
The app is our growth engine. Wallet sign-ups are up 300 percent. Please don't tell me compliance wants to switch it off.
Nobody is switching anything off, Kamran. We are going to see the risk clearly, then put the controls where the danger actually is.
That is the risk-based approach. From the Watchtower you see the whole landscape. Let's teach our newcomer to read it.

cards.title: The risk-based approach in four moves

scenes.heading: You can't check everything equally
scenes.narration: No bank can treat every customer with maximum suspicion. The risk-based approach, FATF's very first Recommendation, says: understand your risks, then put stronger controls where risk is higher and simpler ones where it is genuinely lower.

scenes.heading: Inherent risk
scenes.narration: Inherent risk is the danger before any controls: who your customers are, what you sell, where you operate and how you reach people. Think of it as threat, times vulnerability, times consequence.

scenes.heading: Controls
scenes.narration: Controls are what you do about it: due diligence, screening, monitoring, limits, approvals, training and audit. But only controls that actually work reduce risk. A beautifully designed control that nobody applies reduces nothing.

scenes.heading: Residual risk versus appetite
scenes.narration: What is left after working controls is residual risk. The board sets a risk appetite, and residual risk must fit inside it. If it doesn't, you strengthen controls, limit the product, or exit.

scenes.heading: What the RBA is not
scenes.narration: It is not permission to do less, and it is not zero tolerance. Some duties never switch off, like sanctions screening and reporting suspicion. And it is never a one-time exercise.

cards.title: Building the enterprise-wide risk assessment
cards.caption: The EWRA covers ML, TF and PF, is approved at senior level, and is refreshed whenever something material changes.

items.label: Gather internal data
items.detail: Customer mix, PEPs, NPOs, cash intensity, country flows, channels, alert and STR statistics, audit findings.

items.label: Add external inputs
items.detail: Pakistan's national risk assessment plus FMU and FATF typologies and sector assessments.

items.label: Rate inherent risk
items.detail: Customers, products, geographies and channels, assessing ML, TF and PF explicitly.

items.label: Test control effectiveness
items.detail: Use evidence from testing and audit, not assumptions about design.

items.label: Compare residual with appetite
items.detail: Board-approved appetite decides what is acceptable.

items.label: Act with owners and deadlines
items.detail: Strengthen controls, set limits, add resources or exit segments.

items.label: Approve, share, refresh
items.detail: Senior approval; update for new products, corridors, NRA findings or incidents.

cards.question: The bank's account-opening controls are well designed on paper, but a quality review finds that 40 percent of high-risk corporate files have no beneficial owner recorded. How should residual risk for that segment be judged?
options: Low, because the control design is strong
High, because controls that don't work in practice don't reduce risk
Unchanged until SBP inspects and confirms the finding
Inherent risk should be lowered to reflect the strong design
cards.explanation: Residual risk depends on how controls actually perform. Evidence of failure means risk is not being reduced as designed. Inherent risk never changes because of controls, and the bank must assess its own risk without waiting for an inspection.

cards.title: Four lenses on risk
cards.prompt: Match each risk factor to the example from the bank's portfolio that best illustrates it.

pairs.right: A newly elected member of a provincial assembly, or a cash-heavy used-car dealer
A new instant international transfer feature in the mobile app
A remittance corridor to a country subject to UN Security Council sanctions
New branches in districts the national risk assessment flags for cross-border smuggling
A wallet provider relying on agents paid per sign-up to onboard customers in remote areas

cards.title: The residual risk matrix
cards.caption: Inherent risk alone doesn't decide your response. How well your controls actually work does.

items.label: Low residual
items.detail: Low inherent risk, tested controls. Standard or simplified measures; keep monitoring.

items.label: Watch closely
items.detail: High inherent risk held down by controls proven to work. Keep testing them.

items.label: Hidden gap
items.detail: Low inherent risk but weak controls. Fix gaps before the business grows.

items.label: Act now
items.detail: High inherent risk, weak controls. Strengthen, limit the product or exit.

cards.title: Higher risk, lower risk or not at all?
cards.prompt: Sort each relationship. Higher risk means accept with enhanced measures; outside appetite means the bank must not accept it.
buckets: Lower risk: lighter measures may fit

items.text: A shell bank with no physical presence seeking a correspondent account
A foreign PEP with a well-documented source of wealth
A salaried employee of a known employer opening a low-limit basic account
Someone asking for an anonymous or fictitious-name account
A jeweller with heavy cash turnover
A domestic NPO operating in an area of TF concern
A government department receiving budget releases
An applicant whose identity cannot be verified
A scrap metal dealer paying many unbanked suppliers in cash

cards.title: Kamran's two requests
cards.setting: Kamran's office, 4 pm. He has two printouts ready.

lines.text: Two quick favours. First, Mr Saleem, a property developer, is rated high risk. Respected family, and the EDD questions annoy him. Make him medium.
Have any of his risk factors changed?
No, but he brings us a billion rupees in deposits. Second favour: an exchange company was fined last week. Let's exit all exchange companies. Clean sweep.
Most of our exchange company clients have strong controls and clean histories. If we push them out, where does that money go?
Into hawala, where nobody sees anything. Both requests sound like risk management. Neither is. Let's look at why.

cards.title: The downgrade request
cards.situation: Kamran's request is formally logged: downgrade Mr Saleem, a property developer, from high to medium risk so that he moves from annual EDD reviews to a three-year cycle. The file shows no change in his risk factors: heavy cash receipts from plot buyers, several related companies, and a source of wealth still only partly evidenced. Kamran notes that the client is 'from a very respected family'. You draft compliance's response.

choices.text: Approve. Relationship managers know their clients best, and he is a major depositor.
choices.outcome: At the next SBP inspection the override is sampled. There is no risk-based reason on file, only the RM's view. It is cited as a classic improper override, and the bank must re-review every override from the past two years.

choices.text: Refuse. Overrides need a documented risk-based reason; social standing, size and customer annoyance are not reasons, and review frequency follows the rating.
choices.outcome: Kamran is unhappy, but Ayesha backs you. The file stays high risk, and Hamza helps the RM gather better source-of-wealth evidence so the next review is smoother for the client. Defensible and correct.

choices.text: Downgrade to medium on paper, but quietly keep collecting full EDD in case of inspection.
choices.outcome: This creates a rating that doesn't match the risk and a file that contradicts itself. Monitoring thresholds drop to medium levels, and inspectors treat this as the same improper override, plus a records problem.

choices.text: Approve temporarily for six months, then review.
choices.outcome: Better than a permanent downgrade, but a temporary override without a risk reason is still an override without a risk reason. The flaw is the same.

cards.title: De-risking versus risk management
cards.caption: FATF warns against blanket exits. Decide case by case and exit only when risk can't be managed within appetite.

items.label: Scope
items.left: Exit every exchange company, NPO or district
items.right: Assess each customer on its own risk and controls

items.label: Where money goes
items.left: Pushed into hawala and hundi, unseen

items.label: Who is hurt
items.left: Legitimate users, charities and financial inclusion
items.right: Only customers whose risk truly can't be managed

items.label: Intelligence
items.left: Less information for the FMU and law enforcement

items.label: New risky areas
items.right: Update the risk assessment and calibrate branch controls

cards.title: Hamza's override log
cards.body:
Three override requests reach Hamza in one week.

**1. State-owned utility, model says 'high'.** Huge volumes and many payees push the score up. But the volumes are normal for its role, ownership is transparent and there is no adverse information. **Approved downward**, reasons documented, approval recorded.

**2. 'He's very respectable', model says 'high'.** No risk factor has changed. **Refused.** Familiarity and complaints are not risk reasons.

**3. Domestic NPO, model says 'low'.** The model averages four equal factors, so a basic account at a local branch dilutes its operations in an area of TF concern. **Upgraded**, and Hamza asks for the model to let serious factors, such as TF exposure, PEP status or sanctions links, drive the rating on their own.

**Hamza's test:** could I explain this rating to an inspector in two sentences, using what's on file?

cards.front: A low-risk customer just won a provincial assembly seat. Wait for the scheduled review?
cards.back: No. Becoming a PEP is a trigger event: re-rate now and apply enhanced measures. Also re-rate on adverse media, an STR, sharp activity changes or ownership changes.

cards.front: Simplified due diligence means we skip identification.
cards.back: Myth. SDD lightens some measures where risk is demonstrably low, but customers are still identified, screened and monitored. SDD is never allowed where there is suspicion.

cards.front: Low risk means we can skip sanctions screening.
cards.back: Myth. Sanctions and proscription screening, and reporting suspicion, apply whatever the rating.

cards.front: A customer banked with us for 5+ years qualifies for SDD.
cards.back: Myth. Length of relationship alone doesn't prove low risk.

cards.front: Our EWRA only needs updating when SBP asks.
cards.back: Myth. Update it on material change: new products like wallets, new corridors, new national findings or a major incident.

cards.front: Some customers are not 'high risk' but simply unacceptable.
cards.back: Fact. Shell banks, anonymous accounts, designated persons and customers whose identity can't be verified fall outside any appetite.

cards.title: Launching a product the RBA way
cards.prompt: The digital team wants to launch instant international transfers in the app. Put the steps in the right order.
steps: Describe the product's features: speed, limits, corridors, who can use it
Assess its ML, TF and PF risks before launch
Design controls to match: verification tiers, limits, screening and monitoring scenarios
Obtain senior management approval of the risk assessment
Review risk and controls against live data, then adjust

cards.question: To hit year-end targets, the wallet team proposes doubling transfer limits for customers onboarded through agents, with no change to verification. What is the strongest risk-based response?
options: Approve, because tiered limits are allowed in Pakistan
Ask the FMU to approve the new limits
Raise limits only alongside stronger verification and monitoring, since higher limits increase mule risk
Rate every agent-onboarded customer high risk and freeze their wallets
cards.explanation: Under the RBA, a change that increases risk needs matching controls. Higher limits on weakly verified, agent-onboarded wallets raise mule and fraud exposure. The FMU does not approve product limits, and blanket high ratings or freezes ignore actual risk.

cards.title: Simplified measures and what never switches off
cards.body:
Pakistan's **tiered** accounts and wallets let low-income customers open accounts easily, with limits that keep risk low. Beyond the limits, fuller due diligence is needed to move up a tier.

**Simplified due diligence (SDD)** may fit only where risk is genuinely low and regulations allow it. It means lighter measures, not none.

**Never switched off, whatever the rating:**
- identifying the customer
- sanctions and proscription screening
- monitoring, and reporting suspicion if it arises

**SDD is ruled out** the moment there is suspicion of ML/TF or a specific higher-risk factor. Check your regulator's current rules on which products qualify.

cards.question: A year after a bank exited all its exchange company clients, analysts see more unexplained cash and transfers linked to informal money transfer flowing through ordinary retail accounts. What best explains this?
options: Exchange companies are unregulated, so the exit made no difference
Blanket de-risking pushed legitimate flows into informal channels that now pass unseen through retail accounts
Retail customers have started filing defensive STRs
The bank should have exited retail customers too
cards.explanation: FATF warns that de-risking drives activity into less transparent channels. Exchange companies are licensed and supervised by SBP; informal transfer often settles through ordinary accounts. The exit removed visibility without managing risk.

cards.title: Make the assessment useful, not decorative
cards.body: A 200-page risk assessment with no data, never updated after a major launch and unknown to branch managers impresses nobody. Keep findings short and data-based, link each to an action with an owner and a deadline, and share a one-page summary so branches know the top risks in their area.

cards.title: Watchtower conquered
items: Inherent risk minus controls that actually work gives residual risk, which must fit the board-approved appetite.
The EWRA uses internal data, the national risk assessment and typologies; covers ML, TF and PF; and is updated on material change.
Customer, product, geography and channel factors combine; a serious factor should be able to drive the rating on its own.
Re-rate on triggers such as becoming a PEP; overrides need a documented risk reason and approval; review frequency follows the rating.
New products are risk-assessed before launch; risk-increasing changes need matching controls.
SDD only where risk is truly low and never with suspicion; screening and reporting never switch off; de-risking whole sectors is not risk management.

cards.prompt: Pick one product or customer segment you deal with. What makes it risky, which controls genuinely reduce that risk today, and which control do you suspect looks good on paper but would fail if an inspector sampled ten files?

quiz.question: Which statement best describes 'residual risk'?
options: The risk created by customers who were onboarded before the current policy and have not yet been reviewed
The risk that exists before any controls are applied
The risk that remains after controls have been applied, to be compared with risk appetite
The risk that the regulator will impose a monetary penalty after finding weaknesses during an on-site inspection
quiz.explanation: Residual risk is what remains once controls are applied, and it is compared with the board-approved risk appetite. Risk before controls is inherent risk. Legacy customers and penalty risk are separate concepts.

quiz.question: A microfinance bank is preparing its enterprise-wide risk assessment. Which input is most important to include from outside the institution?
options: Pakistan's national risk assessment and relevant FMU and FATF typologies
Competitor banks' marketing brochures
The bank's annual profit forecast, so that risk ratings stay aligned with business growth targets
Customer satisfaction survey results
quiz.explanation: The national risk assessment and typologies tell the institution which threats are most relevant in Pakistan and how criminals operate. Profit forecasts, brochures and satisfaction surveys say nothing about ML/TF/PF threats.

quiz.question: Mehwish, a relationship manager, asks compliance to downgrade a wealthy property developer from high to medium risk because 'he is a respected family and EDD annoys him'. The customer's risk factors have not changed. What should compliance do?
options: Approve the downgrade because relationship managers know their clients best
Approve it temporarily and review after six months
Downgrade the rating to medium but quietly keep collecting the full EDD file in case of a future inspection
Refuse: an override needs a documented risk-based reason, and social standing or customer inconvenience is not one
quiz.explanation: Overrides must be justified by risk factors, documented and approved. Social standing and customer annoyance do not reduce ML/TF risk, and downgrading to avoid EDD is a recognised control failure. A temporary or cosmetic downgrade has the same flaw.

quiz.question: Which situation best illustrates delivery channel risk?
options: A customer who is a domestic PEP
A wallet provider relying on paid agents to onboard customers in remote areas
A customer sending money from Pakistan to a country that is subject to UN Security Council sanctions
A business customer dealing in used cars
quiz.explanation: Channel risk concerns how customers are reached and served. Reliance on paid agents adds risk because the institution depends on a third party's diligence and incentives. PEP status and business type are customer factors; the sanctioned country is a geographic factor.

quiz.question: A bank launches a new instant international transfer feature in its mobile app. What does FATF expect before launch?
options: An assessment of the ML/TF risks of the new product and appropriate controls to manage them
Approval from the FMU for the product design
Nothing further, provided every existing customer who will use the feature has already completed full CDD
A commitment to file a currency transaction report with the FMU for every international transfer made through the app
quiz.explanation: New products, practices and technologies must be risk-assessed before launch, with controls to manage the identified risks. The FMU does not approve products, existing CDD does not cover new product risks, and CTRs relate to cash transactions.

quiz.question: Faisal Awan, a customer rated low risk two years ago, has just been elected to a provincial assembly. What should happen to his risk rating?
options: It stays low until the next scheduled periodic review, when his new public role can be considered alongside other changes
It changes only if he starts transacting in cash
It should be reassessed now, because becoming a PEP is a trigger event requiring immediate re-rating and enhanced measures
It is automatically closed because PEPs cannot hold accounts
quiz.explanation: Becoming a PEP is a trigger for immediate re-rating rather than waiting for the scheduled review. PEPs can hold accounts subject to enhanced measures; cash activity is not the only reason to reassess.

quiz.question: Which statement about simplified due diligence (SDD) is correct?
options: SDD means the customer does not need to be identified
SDD may apply to genuinely lower-risk situations but never where there is suspicion of ML/TF
SDD applies automatically to all customers who have banked with the institution for more than five years
SDD allows sanctions screening to be skipped for low-value accounts
quiz.explanation: SDD lightens some measures where risk is demonstrably low, but customers are still identified, screened and monitored, and SDD is ruled out when suspicion arises. Length of relationship does not on its own justify SDD.

quiz.question: A bank's AML team finds that its enterprise risk assessment was last updated four years ago, before the bank launched wallets and trade finance for SMEs. What is the main weakness?
options: The assessment should have been prepared by the external auditor
The assessment only needs to be updated when SBP specifically requests it during an inspection or thematic review
Wallets and SME trade finance are low-risk products, so the existing assessment did not need to be updated for them
The assessment no longer reflects the bank's actual risks, so controls may not match them
quiz.explanation: Material changes such as new products must trigger an update, otherwise monitoring, CDD and training are calibrated to an outdated risk picture. Management owns the assessment, not the external auditor, and wallets and trade finance carry significant risks.

quiz.question: Why does FATF warn against wholesale de-risking of sectors such as exchange companies or charities?
options: It can push activity into unregulated channels and exclude legitimate users, without managing the actual risk involved
Because these sectors are legally exempt from AML/CFT controls
Because banks must accept every customer who presents a valid CNIC
Because de-risking sharply increases the number of defensive STRs filed by banks, overloading the FMU's analysts
quiz.explanation: Blanket exits drive money into unmonitored channels such as hawala and harm financial inclusion and humanitarian work, while doing nothing to assess actual risk. These sectors are not exempt, and banks can decline individual customers whose risk is unmanageable.

quiz.question: Which of these is outside any acceptable risk appetite, rather than simply 'high risk'?
options: A foreign PEP with a well-documented source of wealth
A shell bank seeking a correspondent account
A jeweller with heavy cash turnover
A non-resident Pakistani opening an account through a digital channel
quiz.explanation: Shell banks have no physical presence and no meaningful supervision, and correspondent relationships with them are prohibited. PEPs, jewellers and non-resident customers can be accepted with appropriate, sometimes enhanced, due diligence.

sessions.title: Customer Due Diligence: Knowing Who Is Really There
sessions.summary: Every relationship passes through the gatehouse. Learn to identify and verify customers, find the natural persons behind companies and trusts, choose between simplified, standard and enhanced measures, and handle PEPs, NPOs, correspondent relationships and record keeping.
objectives: List the elements of customer due diligence and when it must be performed
Identify and verify individuals and legal persons using Pakistani documents and NADRA verification
Trace beneficial ownership through layered structures to the natural persons who own or control them
Apply enhanced due diligence to PEPs, NPOs, correspondent banking and other higher-risk relationships
Explain what records must be kept, why, and what to do when CDD cannot be completed

cards.title: Who is really behind Zarnab?
cards.setting: The Gatehouse: the onboarding review room. Wednesday morning.

lines.text: Remember Zarnab Trading, where the Karachi wallets sent their money? It has just applied to us for an import LC facility.
Director and 30 percent shareholder: Shahid Rana. The other 70 percent belongs to Crescent Star FZE, a company in a Gulf free zone.
A company can't be the real owner. Somewhere behind Crescent Star there is a human being. Our job at the Gatehouse is to find them.
(on the line) And a confession from Multan: we opened Irfan's account and three of the depositors' accounts. All passed NADRA biometrics perfectly.
One of them told my officer he was a daily-wage labourer, yet expected PKR 5 million a month in cash. Nobody asked a follow-up question.
Biometrics tell you who someone is, not whether their money is clean. Today you learn to know who is really there.

cards.title: Customer due diligence in five scenes

scenes.heading: Element one: identify and verify
scenes.narration: Find out who the customer is and verify it with reliable, independent sources: CNIC or NICOP, NADRA biometric checks, Verisys. People acting for the customer, like signatories and attorneys, are verified too.

scenes.heading: Element two: the beneficial owner
scenes.narration: Identify the natural person who ultimately owns or controls the customer, and take risk-based steps to verify them. Never stop at a company name.

scenes.heading: Element three: purpose and nature
scenes.narration: Understand what the account is for: expected volumes, source of funds, main counterparties and countries. Without this profile, nothing later can look unusual.

scenes.heading: Element four: ongoing due diligence
scenes.narration: Keep watching activity against that profile and keep the information current. CDD is not a form you fill once.

scenes.heading: When CDD is required
scenes.narration: When a relationship starts, for occasional transactions above regulatory thresholds including certain wires, whenever you suspect ML or TF whatever the amount, and when you doubt earlier information.

scenes.heading: Identity is not legitimacy
scenes.narration: A labourer who passes biometrics but expects five million rupees a month in cash is a question, not an approval. Ask about the source and purpose, and escalate if the answer doesn't fit.

cards.title: The due diligence pyramid
cards.caption: Depth of CDD follows risk. The narrow top is a small group of customers you must not accept at all.

items.label: Decline
items.detail: Shell banks, anonymous accounts, designated persons, identity or ownership that can't be established.

items.label: Enhanced due diligence
items.detail: Foreign PEPs, higher-risk domestic PEPs, correspondents, high-risk jurisdictions: senior approval, source of wealth and funds, closer monitoring.

items.label: Standard CDD
items.detail: Most customers: full identification, beneficial owner, purpose and nature, screening, ongoing monitoring.

items.label: Simplified due diligence
items.detail: Genuinely low risk only, such as tiered low-limit accounts where rules allow; never with suspicion.

cards.question: A trainee lists what she thinks are the core elements of CDD. Which item on her list is wrong?
options: Understanding the purpose and intended nature of the relationship
Obtaining the customer's agreement before any suspicious transaction report is filed
Identifying the beneficial owner
Conducting ongoing due diligence
cards.explanation: The four elements are identification and verification, beneficial ownership, purpose and nature, and ongoing due diligence. Customers have no say in STRs; telling them a report is being considered would be tipping off.

cards.title: From paper owners to the real person
cards.caption: A beneficial owner is always a natural person. Keep looking through layers until you find one.

items.label: Registered shareholders
items.detail: The names on the share register, which may be companies, trusts or nominees.

items.label: Intermediate companies
items.detail: Look through every corporate layer, at home and abroad.

items.label: Trusts and nominees
items.detail: Find settlor, trustees, protector, beneficiaries and anyone with effective control.

items.label: The natural person
items.detail: The human who ultimately owns or controls the customer.

cards.title: Run the beneficial ownership cascade
cards.prompt: Put the steps for identifying a company's beneficial owner in the correct order.
steps: Trace ownership through every layer to natural persons and test them against the ownership threshold in the current regulations
If ownership doesn't reveal who controls, identify people with control by other means, such as power to appoint the board
Only if no one is found, record the senior managing official and document what you did
Verify the people identified on a risk basis, using registries and independent sources
Screen every beneficial owner and factor the results into the customer's risk rating

cards.title: Unwrapping Crescent Star
cards.setting: Hamza's desk, two days later. Registry extracts are spread everywhere.

lines.text: Crescent Star FZE is wholly owned by a family trust. The trustee is a professional trust company. That alone tells us nothing.
But the trust deed gives the settlor, Tariq Lodhi of Lahore, the power to replace the trustee and direct investments. He controls the 70 percent.
Good. So the beneficial owners are Shahid Rana with 30 percent and Tariq Lodhi through the trust. We also identify the trust's beneficiaries.
One more thing. Screening shows Shahid Rana is a long-time business partner of a sitting provincial minister.
Then he is a close associate of a domestic PEP. That makes source of wealth central. And remember that 'family gift' from the Gulf in our file?
PKR 30 million, sent to Shahid Rana, described as a gift. It landed the week Zarnab applied.

cards.question: A Pakistani company is owned: 22% by Ms Hina, 18% by Mr Asim, and 60% by a holding company that is owned 50/50 by Mr Faraz and Mr Junaid. Nobody has special control rights. Assuming a 25% threshold, who are the beneficial owners?
options: The holding company, as the largest shareholder
Ms Hina only, as the largest individual shareholder
Mr Faraz and Mr Junaid, who each own 30% indirectly
All four individuals equally
cards.explanation: Look through the holding company: each of Mr Faraz and Mr Junaid owns half of 60%, which is 30% indirectly, above the threshold. Ms Hina (22%) and Mr Asim (18%) are below it and have no control rights, though they are still recorded as shareholders. A company can never be a beneficial owner.

cards.title: PEPs: power creates risk
cards.body:
A **politically exposed person** holds or has held a prominent public function: ministers, legislators, senior judges, senior military officers and civil servants, heads of state-owned enterprises, senior party officials.

- **Foreign PEPs:** enhanced measures **always**: senior management approval, source of wealth **and** source of funds, enhanced monitoring.
- **Domestic and international-organisation PEPs:** the same measures when the relationship is higher risk. Check whether your regulator requires more.
- **Family members and close associates** are treated as PEPs, because they often hold corrupt assets.
- **Status doesn't expire automatically.** Declassifying a former PEP is a risk-based decision, not a fixed time limit.

Being a PEP is not a crime. The aim is to check their money matches their legitimate wealth.

cards.front: Source of funds vs source of wealth
cards.back: Source of funds: where the money in this transaction or relationship comes from. Source of wealth: how the customer built their overall net worth.

cards.front: A trust applies. Whom do you identify?
cards.back: The settlor, trustees, any protector, the beneficiaries or class of beneficiaries, and anyone else with effective control.

cards.front: A federal secretary retired three years ago. Still a PEP?
cards.back: Possibly. Decide on risk, considering his former role and lingering influence, not a fixed period.

cards.front: Customer shows an expired CNIC and a NADRA renewal token
cards.back: Follow your bank's current procedure and SBP instructions on expired identity documents. Don't improvise, and don't open it in a relative's name.

cards.front: A shop declares turnover far above similar shops
cards.back: Verify the business itself, for example with a site visit and sales evidence, before agreeing the expected profile. Papers prove existence, not scale.

cards.front: A review reveals a new foreign parent owning 70%, never disclosed
cards.back: Identify, verify and screen the new beneficial owners, re-rate the customer, and consider why the change was hidden.

cards.title: Higher-risk relationships: what each needs
cards.prompt: Match each relationship to the measure the standards expect.

pairs.right: EDD in every case: senior approval, source of wealth and funds, enhanced monitoring

pairs.left: PEP's adult son receiving a large 'gift'
pairs.right: Treat as a PEP and establish how the father built the wealth behind the gift
Screen office bearers; understand implementing partners and how and where funds are used
Assess its business, supervision and controls; senior approval; no shell banks; understand any nested banks
Follow policy: request the data, reject or suspend, and consider whether it is suspicious

cards.title: A namesake on the trustee list
cards.situation: One of the Karachi wallets in the trail sends money to a welfare trust in Swat, which now applies for its own account. One trustee shares a name and father's name with a person on the Fourth Schedule of the Anti-Terrorism Act. The trust is properly registered and runs a small clinic. The branch wants to open the account today. What do you do?

choices.text: Open it. The trust is registered and doing welfare work.
choices.outcome: Registration doesn't cure the risk. If the trustee is the listed person, the bank may now be making funds available to a proscribed person, a serious breach.

choices.text: Compare identifiers such as CNIC and date of birth against the list, and escalate to compliance before anything is opened.
choices.outcome: The CNIC on the published list differs from the trustee's, and his date of birth is 18 years apart. Compliance documents the comparison, clears the namesake and continues normal NPO due diligence. Right approach.

choices.text: Ask the trustee directly whether he is the listed person, and proceed if he denies it.
choices.outcome: If he is the listed person, you have just warned him. And a denial proves nothing. Identifiers resolve matches; questions to the customer don't.

choices.text: Ask the trust to remove that trustee's name from the account documents, then proceed.
choices.outcome: This hides a person who controls the customer. Beneficial ownership and control can't be edited away to make a file look clean.

cards.title: The 'gift' and the word 'business'
cards.body:
Shahid Rana is now a close associate of a domestic PEP, and the PKR 30 million 'family gift' arrived from the Gulf just before Zarnab's application.

The relationship manager's EDD note on his source of wealth reads: **'business'**.

Ayesha sends it back. Acceptable EDD would explain:
- **what** the business is, and his real role in it
- **how** the wealth was built over time, and whether it fits his known income
- **who** sent the gift, how the sender made that money, and why it was given
- **what independent evidence** supports each point: accounts, tax returns, property records

A countersignature adds approval, not substance. Senior management approval is needed to proceed, and if the answers don't add up, the right question becomes whether to file an STR.

cards.question: During account opening, Rukhsana's officer becomes strongly suspicious that the applicant is a mule for fraud proceeds. More detailed questions would clearly alert him. What do the standards allow?
options: Open the account quietly and report next year
Explain to the applicant that compliance has concerns
Finish every CDD question regardless of the tipping-off risk
Stop the CDD process and escalate so an STR can be filed
cards.explanation: Where pursuing CDD would tip off the customer, institutions may stop the process and file an STR instead. Voicing concerns is tipping off, and opening the account and delaying the report defeats both CDD and prompt reporting.

cards.title: Would this file survive an inspector?
cards.prompt: Sort each CDD file entry: good enough, or a gap an inspector would flag?

items.text: Beneficial owner recorded as 'Crescent Star FZE'
Beneficial owner traced through the trust to the settlor who controls it
Labourer expecting PKR 5m cash a month, opened after biometrics with no questions
Correspondent bank onboarded on its own signed questionnaire alone
Source of wealth explained with business history, tax returns and property records
Signatory acting under a power of attorney identified and verified
Account opened first, respondent bank to be assessed 'within a year'
NPO file lists implementing partners and where funds are spent

cards.title: Records: the numbers that matter
cards.caption: Confirm exact periods and starting points in current AMLA provisions and your regulator's regulations.

items.label: FATF minimum
items.detail: A floor for the global standard, not Pakistan's rule.

items.label: Pakistan, main records
items.detail: Law and regulations require longer retention for CDD and transaction records.

items.label: Accounts still covered
items.detail: Retention runs on after the relationship ends.

items.label: Retrieval
items.detail: Records must be found quickly when lawfully requested.

cards.title: When CDD can't be completed
cards.body:
If you can't identify or verify the customer, find the beneficial owner or understand the purpose of the relationship:

- **Don't open** the account or carry out the transaction.
- For an existing customer, **consider ending** the relationship under policy.
- **Consider an STR**: refusal to explain, like 'our investors value privacy', may itself be suspicious.

**Keep:** identity documents, verification results, ownership information, account files and correspondence, transaction records detailed enough to reconstruct each transaction, internal suspicion reports and decisions, STRs and CTRs, and screening results with how matches were resolved. Keep records longer if an investigation or case is ongoing.

cards.title: Gatehouse unlocked
items: CDD has four elements: identify and verify, beneficial owner, purpose and nature, ongoing due diligence. Biometrics confirm identity, not legitimacy.
A beneficial owner is always a natural person: look through every layer, then control by other means, then the senior managing official as a last resort.
Foreign PEPs always need EDD; domestic PEPs when higher risk; family and close associates count; declassification is risk-based.
Source of wealth explains net worth, source of funds explains this money; 'business' is never an EDD answer.
Resolve name matches with identifiers, not by asking the customer; stop CDD and report if questions would tip someone off.
Keep records well beyond FATF's five-year minimum, including for closed accounts; if CDD can't be completed, don't open and consider an STR.

cards.prompt: Recall a customer file that looked complete but told you little about what the customer actually does or where their money comes from. Which two questions would have turned it into a genuinely useful CDD file?

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the core elements of customer due diligence?
options: Identifying and verifying the customer
Identifying the beneficial owner
Understanding the purpose and intended nature of the relationship
Obtaining the customer's written consent before any STR is filed
quiz.explanation: The core elements are identification and verification, beneficial ownership, purpose and nature, and ongoing monitoring. Customer consent has no role in STR filing; telling the customer about an STR would be tipping off.

quiz.question: Saima opens an account for a customer whose CNIC passes NADRA biometric verification. The customer says he is a labourer, yet expects to deposit PKR 5 million a month in cash. What is the best next step?
options: Open the account as the biometric check confirms the customer is genuine
Ask about the source and purpose of the expected funds, and escalate internally if the explanation does not fit his profile
Refuse the account immediately and file a CTR
Open the account and wait to see whether the deposits actually happen before asking him any questions about them
quiz.explanation: Biometrics confirm identity, not legitimacy. The mismatch between occupation and expected cash must be explored and escalated if unexplained. Opening without questions ignores a clear red flag, and a CTR is a threshold report for actual cash transactions, not a refusal mechanism.

quiz.question: Which description of a beneficial owner is correct?
options: The company or trust that is the registered shareholder of the customer
Any person authorised to operate the customer's account
The natural person who ultimately owns or controls the customer
The bank officer responsible for the relationship
quiz.explanation: A beneficial owner is always a natural person who ultimately owns or controls the customer. A registered corporate shareholder is a legal owner, and signatories are authorised persons who may or may not be beneficial owners.

quiz.question: For a family trust, which group of people should be identified as part of beneficial ownership?
options: The settlor, the trustees, any protector, the beneficiaries or class of beneficiaries, and anyone else with effective control
Only the trustee, because the trustee holds legal title to the trust assets and signs all the account documents
Only the beneficiaries, because they will receive the assets
Only the lawyer who drafted the trust deed
quiz.explanation: For trusts, all parties who may own or control the arrangement must be identified: settlor, trustees, protector, beneficiaries and anyone with effective control. Focusing only on the trustee or beneficiaries leaves gaps; the drafting lawyer is not a party.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes 'source of wealth' as distinct from 'source of funds'?
options: Source of wealth is the specific bank account or instrument from which a payment is made, and source of funds is the customer's net worth
Source of wealth only applies to companies and other legal persons, while source of funds applies to individual customers
They are the same and the terms can be used interchangeably
Source of wealth explains how total net worth was built; source of funds explains the money in a given transaction
quiz.explanation: Source of funds concerns the money used in this relationship or transaction; source of wealth concerns how the customer accumulated their overall wealth. The distinction matters most for PEPs and high-net-worth clients.

quiz.question: Daniyal, a former federal secretary who retired three years ago, applies for a private banking relationship. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Treat him as a standard customer, because PEP status automatically ends on retirement and three full years have now passed since he left office
Assess his PEP risk on a risk basis, considering his former role and influence, rather than assuming status has lapsed
Decline the relationship, because former senior officials cannot open private banking accounts for a period after retirement
Treat only his family members as PEPs, not him
quiz.explanation: PEP declassification is risk-based, not automatic after a fixed period. A former senior official may retain influence and corruption risk. Declining outright is not required; enhanced measures can manage the risk.

quiz.question: A local welfare trust in Swat applies for an account. One of its trustees shares a name and father's name with a person listed in the Fourth Schedule of the ATA 1997. What should happen before the account is opened?
options: Check identifiers such as CNIC and date of birth to resolve the match, and escalate to compliance
Open the account because the trust is registered and provides welfare services
Remove the trustee's name from the account documents and proceed
Ask the trustee directly whether he is the person listed in the Fourth Schedule, record his answer and proceed if he denies it
quiz.explanation: A potential match must be resolved using identifiers such as CNIC and date of birth and escalated to compliance; a true match means the funds must not be made available. Registration does not cure the risk, removing the name hides a controller, and asking the trustee tips him off and is unreliable.

quiz.question: When a Pakistani bank provides correspondent services to a foreign respondent bank, which of these is required?
options: Treating the respondent as low risk if it is in a FATF member country
Relying on the respondent's own AML/CFT compliance certificate and questionnaire, signed by its chief compliance officer
Assessing the respondent's business, controls and supervision, obtaining senior management approval, and excluding shell banks
Opening the account first and assessing the respondent within one year
quiz.explanation: Correspondent relationships require assessment of the respondent's business, supervision and AML/CFT controls, senior management approval, clear responsibilities and a shell bank prohibition. FATF membership does not make a bank low risk, and a self-certificate alone is not enough.

quiz.question: During account opening, Nimra develops a strong suspicion that the applicant is laundering fraud proceeds. Continuing to ask detailed CDD questions would likely alert him. What do the standards permit?
options: Opening the account to avoid suspicion, then filing an STR next year
Telling the applicant politely that compliance has concerns about him
Completing all CDD first, regardless of the tipping-off risk
Stopping the CDD process and escalating so that an STR can be filed
quiz.explanation: Where pursuing CDD would tip off the customer, institutions may stop the process and file an STR instead. Telling him about concerns is tipping off, and opening the account and delaying the report defeats both CDD and prompt reporting.

quiz.question: An inspector asks a branch to produce the CDD file and transaction records for a customer whose account was closed six years ago. The branch says the records were destroyed after five years under the FATF minimum. What is the issue?
options: The branch likely breached Pakistan's longer record retention requirement, which goes beyond FATF's five-year minimum
There is no issue, because FATF's minimum period has passed
There is no issue, because closed accounts are outside record-keeping rules
The only issue is that the branch should have scanned the records before destroying the paper files
quiz.explanation: FATF's five years is a minimum; Pakistan's law and regulations require longer retention for the main CDD and transaction records. Closed accounts remain covered, and scanning is irrelevant if the records were destroyed before the required period ended.

sessions.title: Monitoring, Red Flags and Reporting to the FMU
sessions.summary: At the listening post you learn to hear what transactions are saying. Recognise red flags in branches, trade, remittances and digital channels, investigate alerts properly, escalate internally, and report STRs and CTRs to the FMU without tipping off the customer.
objectives: Explain how ongoing and transaction monitoring work and how alerts should be investigated and closed
Recognise red flags for branch cash activity, money mules, trade-based money laundering, remittances and digital channels
Decide when an STR is required and write a clear, useful STR narrative
Distinguish STRs from CTRs and explain the reporting route to the FMU
Apply the tipping-off prohibition and the internal escalation process

cards.title: The alert queue lights up
cards.setting: The Listening Post: the monitoring room, 8:45 am. Three screens, one chai each.

lines.text: Overnight alerts. Irfan Bhatti's account: 41 cash deposits in three weeks, nearly all between PKR 450,000 and 490,000, at seven branches.
And the Karachi wallets: one opened through the app last week received 37 small transfers from strangers in two days. Each was moved out within minutes.
(on the line) It gets better. Yesterday Irfan asked my teller, 'How much cash can I deposit without the bank reporting it?'
What did the teller say?
Nothing yet. She came straight to me. She's nervous about getting it wrong.
Good instinct. Today is about hearing what transactions are saying, and reporting it right without letting the customer know.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of ears
scenes.narration: Monitoring compares what a customer does with what CDD told us to expect. Systems run rules tuned to our risk assessment, and people notice what systems can't, like a depositor who doesn't know the account holder's name.

scenes.heading: Review and gather
scenes.narration: An analyst checks the alert against the profile and history, then gathers more: related accounts, counterparties, past alerts, open sources, and careful routine questions through the relationship manager.

scenes.heading: Decide
scenes.narration: Is there a reasonable explanation, or are there grounds to suspect? Many alerts close legitimately. Filing everything 'to be safe' is defensive filing, and it buries real intelligence.

scenes.heading: Write down why
scenes.narration: 'Customer is genuine, closed' is not a rationale. 'Matches the Eid sales pattern of the last three years, with normal counterparties' is. Someone must be able to check your decision later.

scenes.heading: Backlogs are risk
scenes.narration: An alert reviewed three months late is a report filed three months late. Inspectors treat alert backlogs as a serious finding.

cards.title: Red flag or normal activity?
cards.prompt: Sort each pattern from this week's alerts. Red flags call for a closer look; normal activity can be closed with a rationale.

items.text: Repeated cash deposits just below a threshold, spread across branches
A garment retailer's cash deposits rise before Eid, as in the last three years
A self-described cook receives remittances from 12 unrelated senders and withdraws cash the same day
Monthly salary credits from the same employer
